newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Telecom giants vie for Taiwan's US$3.6 bln market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Telecom giants vie for Taiwan's US$3.6 bln market.

text.p: Seventeen seasoned contenders. Eight winning prizes. And a US$3.6 billion annual purse.
Taiwan's cellular phone sweepstakes is off and running.

In the island's most lucrative and high-profile bidding contest ever, world telecommunication giants are teaming with local business heavyweights to vie for eight operating franchises in Taiwan's newly opened mobile phone sector.
AT&T, Sprint, Southwestern Bell, Mitsubishi, AirTouch and Acer are but a few of the big shots who have formed 17 ventures and submitted 42 applications for the jackpot.
The trail-blazing hopefuls are lured by visions of 11-fold growth in Taiwan's vastly untapped cellular market seen turning in 10 years into a US$3.6 billion-a-year market.

"Since the mobile phone industry has been a closed market for such a long time, it really has very exciting potential for development," Scott Hooper, president of AT&T Wireless Services, told Reuters. "We predict the number of mobile phone users in Taiwan will reach 10 million in 10 years."
That's nearly one mobile phone for every two of Taiwan's 21 million people -- a level of service the state-owned telephone company, a longtime monopoly, could not deliver alone.

Parliament unplugged the monopoly in January when it voted to open several telecom sectors, including mobile telephony, for private and limited foreign investment. Foreign investors can own stakes of up to 20 percent in telecom ventures.
SECTOR'S FIRST BIG OPENING
The mobile phone bidding is the sector's first big opening.
Bidders cautioned, however, that the process would require new levels of openness in issuing the franchise licences to ensure Taiwan gets the best systems possible.

"The government has shown a sincere commitment to reforming the industry, and the presence of major international firms demonstrates our confidence in the government," said Chen Jain-shing, president of Southwestern Bell's Taiwan branch.

"But now that the big players are here, you've got to make the selection process fair and transparent. The government can't allow irregularities because the future of its reputation and the industry is at stake," Chen said.

Next, winning bidders will have to forge delicate and crucial ties with Chunghwa Telecommunications, the state-owned enterprise that was formed in July to take over operations of the old monopoly Directorate General of Telecommunications.

Private ventures compete with Chunghwa's mobile networks for market share, but also will have to pay it for use of its trunk telecom systems rather than create their own -- giving Chunghwa power to dictate operating costs.
Douglas Hsu, chairman of Taiwan's AT&T venture partner the Far Eastern Group, was confident that Chunghwa and private upstarts could manage a peaceful and mutually beneficial co-existence.

"It's in everyone's interest to see the market grow," Hsu said. "The more clients we have, the more networks we have to rent from Chunghwa and the more both parties benefit. It is not in Chunghwa's interest to set unreasonable prices."
AT&T's Hooper said it was not uncommon for his company to face a competitor who also set the rules.
"In the United States we have to rent networks from local phone companies and compete with them at the same time. This issue can be resolved with common sense," he said.

While bidders accept Chunghwa's network monopoly, they are urging the government to make good on a pledge to phase out its so-called profit cap -- a requirement that telecom firms reduce rates if their operating profits exceeded 11.5 percent.
"Such a requirement would simply drive investors out of the market because it defeats the whole purpose of market liberalisation," said Chen of Southwestern Bell.
"You don't need such a regulation to reduce prices. The rates will go down automatically because of increasing competition. That's the way a free market works."
Taiwan agreed to drop the cap in trade talks with the United States in July, but the move still needs parliament's approval.
In the same talks, Taiwan refused to relax a 20 percent limit on foreign ownership, and Chunghwa in particular has objected strongly to further liberalisation of the industry.
LIBERALISATION DEBATE
AT&T, the world's largest cellular operator, said it accepts the need for limits on foreign ownership -- something the United States also practices -- but hopes it gradually will be eased.
"We think 20 percent is a fair level right now, and it is comparable with caps in many other countries we've invested in," said Mark Hamilton, AT&T Wireless vice-president.
"But we hope that as the industry matures, liberalisation will progress further and more restrictions will be lifted."
Chen envisages a future in which Taiwan opens up the basic telecom network itself -- not just mobiles.

"As big as the wireless industry seems, it is only about 30 percent of the total sales revenue in the telecom market, and the real major floodgate will be opened by the other 70 percent in wired telephone services," he said.
Taiwan plans to open all sectors for private investment by 2000 and the mobile liberalisation is seen setting the tone.

"All eyes are on the government and how it handles this transition to private ownership," said Far Eastern's Hsu. "If the results turn out as great as everyone predicts, then everyone will come back for more."

Said AT&T's Hooper: "The possibilities for the telecom industry are limitless with advances in technology and opening up of markets. We hope this is only the beginning of the telecom future in Taiwan."
